'''Henry James Snaith''' (born 1978)<ref name=ch>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2018|url=https://beta.companieshouse.gov.uk/officers/fpZDwTX63MRJDgShNrnqB_xAI5Y/appointments|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190408145614/https://beta.companieshouse.gov.uk/officers/fpZDwTX63MRJDgShNrnqB_xAI5Y/appointments|archive-date=2019-04-08|title=Henry James Snaith|publisher=[[Companies House]]|location=London|website=companieshouse.gov.uk}}</ref> {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} is a professor in [[physics]] in the [[Clarendon Laboratory]] at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=royal/> Research from his group has led to the creation of a new research field, based on halide perovskites for use as solar absorbers. Many individuals who were PhD students and postdoctoral researchers in Snaith's group have now established research groups, independent research portfolios and commercial enterprises. He co-founded [[Oxford Photovoltaics]] in 2010 to commercialise [[perovskite]] based [[tandem solar cell]]s.

==Education==
Snaith was educated at [[Gresham's School]], an independent school in Norfolk, from 1989 to 1996.<ref name=greshams>{{cite web|title=Old Greshamians|url=https://www.greshams.com/old-greshamians/old-greshamians-people/og-science-technology/|website=greshams.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825183915/https://www.greshams.com/old-greshamians/old-greshamians-people/og-science-technology/|archive-date=2017-08-25}}</ref> He completed his undergraduate studies at the [[University of Bristol]], followed by postgraduate research at the [[University of Cambridge]] where he was awarded a PhD in 2005 for research on [[polymer solar cell]]s supervised by [[Richard Friend]].<ref name=friend/><ref name=oxfordpv/><ref name=snaithphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|title=Polymer based photovoltaic diodes|first= Henry James|last=Snaith|year=2005|url=http://ulmss-newton.lib.cam.ac.uk/vwebv/holdingsInfo?bibId=26542|website=lib.cam.ac.uk|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.614761}}|oclc=890157906|publisher=University of Cambridge}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Following his PhD, Snaith did two years of [[postdoctoral research]] with [[Michael Grätzel]] at the [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne]] (EPFL).<ref name=oxfordpv/><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/nl071656u| pmid = 17918905| title = Efficiency Enhancements in Solid-State Hybrid Solar Cells via Reduced Charge Recombination and Increased Light Capture| journal = [[Nano Letters]]| volume = 7| issue = 11| pages = 3372–6| year = 2007| last1 = Snaith | first1 = H. J. | author-link1 = Henry Snaith| last2 = Moule | first2 = A. J. | last3 = Klein | first3 = C. D. | last4 = Meerholz | first4 = K. | last5 = Friend | first5 = R. H. | author-link5 = Richard Friend| last6 = Grätzel | first6 = M. | author-link6 = Michael Grätzel| bibcode = 2007NanoL...7.3372S}}</ref> He returned to the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] as a Junior [[Research Fellow]] at [[Clare College, Cambridge]] in 2006. Following this, Snaith was appointed a [[Research Councils UK]] (RCUK) research fellow while at the University of Oxford,{{Year needed|date=May 2015}} then promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] and Professor.{{Year needed|date=May 2015}} According to a biography from the [[Materials Research Society]] (MRS): {{centred pull quote|His research has been focused on new materials and device architectures for future generation low-cost photovoltaic. Snaith's achievements include the first demonstration of "[[gyroid]]" structured titania for [[Dye-sensitized solar cell|dye solar cells]], the first demonstration of [[mesoporous]] [[single crystal]]s of [[anatase]] [[Titanium dioxide|TiO<sub>2</sub>]] and the recent discovery of high efficiency solid-state organometal trihalide perovskite-based thin film and mesosuperstructured solar cells. In 2010, he founded Oxford Photovoltaics Ltd., which is commercialising [[perovskite solar cell]]s for building integrated and utility scale photovoltaic applications.<ref name=mrsbiog>{{cite web|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140903123607/http://www.mrs.org/oyi-2014-snaith/|archive-date=2014-09-03|title=Outstanding Young Investigator Award 2014|publisher=Materials Research Society|url=http://www.mrs.org/oyi-2014-snaith}}</ref>}}

Snaith's research has been funded by the [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]] (EPSRC).<ref name=gtr>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150523042414/http://gtr.rcuk.ac.uk/person/15E36410-2834-433A-B01F-15A10565CFEC|archive-date=2015-05-23|url=http://gtr.rcuk.ac.uk/person/15E36410-2834-433A-B01F-15A10565CFEC|publisher=[[Research Councils UK]]|title=UK Government Research Grants awarded to Henry Snaith}}</ref> 

===Awards and honours===
Snaith was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2015|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2015]].<ref>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306143408/https://royalsociety.org/people/henry-snaith-12312/ |archive-date=2016-03-06 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/henry-snaith-12312/ |title=Professor Henry Snaith FRS |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London }} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{quote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2016-03-09 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=2015-09-25 }}}}</ref> His certificate of election reads: {{centred pull quote|Professor Henry Snaith has pioneered the development of hybrid materials for energy and [[photovoltaic]]s through an interdisciplinary combination of materials synthesis, device development, advanced optoelectronic characterisations and theoretical studies. He has created new materials with advanced functionality and enhanced understanding of fundamental mechanisms. His recent discovery of extremely efficient [[thin-film solar cell]]s manufactured from organic-inorganic [[Metal halides|metal halide]] [[Perovskite (structure)|perovskite]]s has reset aspirations within the photovoltaics community. His work has started a new field of research, attracting both academic and industrial following, propelled by the prospect of delivering a higher efficiency photovoltaic technology at a much lower cost than existing [[Crystalline silicon|silicon PV]].<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/henry-snaith/ |title =Professor Henry Snaith FRS |publisher=The Royal Society |archive-date=2015-05-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150502204010/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/henry-snaith/ |location=London}}</ref>}}

In 2012, Snaith was [[Institute of Physics]] [[Clifford Paterson Medal and Prize]] for "his important contributions to the field of excitonic solar cells".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/early-career/paterson/medallists/page_56456.html |publisher=Institute of Physics |title=2012 Paterson medal and prize |access-date=22 December 2019 |archive-date=22 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222183539/http://www.iop.org/about/awards/early-career/paterson/medallists/page_56456.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2014, Snaith was awarded the MRS Outstanding [[Principal investigator|Young Investigator]] Award.<ref name=mrs>{{Cite journal| author = Anon | doi = 10.1557/mrs.2014.76| title = Henry J. Snaith named 2014 MRS Outstanding Young Investigator for perovskite hybrid solar cells| journal = MRS Bulletin| volume = 39| issue = 4| pages = 375| year = 2014|publisher=journals.cambridge.org| doi-access = free}}</ref> He was awarded the Patterson Medal of the [[Institute of Physics]] in 2012, and named as one of ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'''s [[Nature's 10|ten people who mattered]] in 2013.<ref name=naturesten/>

In 2015, Snaith was ranked number two on the list of ''The World's Most Influential Scientific Minds'', a citation analysis identifying the scientists who have made the most significant impact within their respective field of study by the [[Intellectual Property]] (IP) and Science business of [[Thomson Reuters]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://stateofinnovation.thomsonreuters.com/worlds-most-influential-scientific-minds-report-2015|website=stateofinnovation.thomsonreuters.com|title=Worlds most influential scientific minds report 2015|access-date=17 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228030959/http://stateofinnovation.thomsonreuters.com/worlds-most-influential-scientific-minds-report-2015|archive-date=28 December 2016|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref> In May 2016, he was awarded the EU-40 Materials Prize from the European Material Research Society.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.european-mrs.com/awards/eu-40-materials-prize|website=european-mrs.com|title=The European Material Research Society|access-date=7 May 2016|archive-date=22 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160422065202/http://www.european-mrs.com/awards/eu-40-materials-prize|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In October 2017, he was awarded the [[Institute of Physics]] [[James Joule Medal and Prize]] for the discovery and development of organic-inorganic metal-halide perovskite solar cells.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/page_69701.html|title=IOP Award Winners 2017|last=Physics|first=Institute of|website=www.iop.org|language=en-GB|access-date=2017-11-15|archive-date=16 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171116032703/http://www.iop.org/about/awards/page_69701.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In September 2020, he was awarded the Becquerel Prize in honour of his contributions to the use of perovskites as solar cells.{{cn|date=September 2023}}
